name: Eisenkot, Gadi
text: Israeli general and politician who was IDF Chief of Staff from 2015 to 2019. He entered politics in 2022 with [[Benny Gantz]]'s National Unity party and sat as an observer in the war cabinet after the [[October 7 attack (2023)]]; his son Gal was killed fighting in Gaza in December 2023. He left National Unity in 2025, founded [[Yashar!]] that September, and led it to 21 seats in the October 2026 election. On November 8, 2026, President [[Isaac Herzog]] gave him the mandate to form a government after 67 Knesset members recommended him.

name: Lapid, Yair
text: Israeli journalist and politician who founded [[Yesh Atid]] in 2012. He was finance minister in 2013–2014, foreign minister and alternate prime minister in the 2021 coalition with [[Naftali Bennett]], and prime minister from July to December 2022. He led the opposition from 2023 until April 2026, when he merged Yesh Atid into Bennett's [[Together (B'Yachad)]] list and took second place on it.

name: Herzog, Isaac
text: Eleventh president of Israel, in office since July 2021, and the son of the sixth president, Chaim Herzog. He led the Labor Party from 2013 to 2017, was opposition leader from 2015 to 2018, and chaired the [[Jewish Agency for Israel]] from 2018 to 2021. After the October 2026 election he held the consultations with the parties and gave [[Gadi Eisenkot]] the mandate to form a government.

name: Liberman, Avigdor
text: Israeli politician born in Soviet Moldova in 1958 who immigrated in 1978 and founded [[Yisrael Beiteinu]] in 1999. He has served as foreign minister, defense minister and finance minister. A secular right-winger, he opposes draft exemptions for ultra-Orthodox men. After the 2026 election he backed [[Gadi Eisenkot]] for prime minister but refused to join a minority government that would depend on Arab parties.

name: Golan, Yair
text: Retired IDF major general and deputy chief of staff from 2014 to 2017 who leads [[Democrats (Israel)]], the party formed in 2024 when Labor and Meretz merged. On the morning of the [[October 7 attack (2023)]] he drove south on his own to rescue survivors of the Nova music festival. The Democrats won eight seats in the 2026 election.

name: Smotrich, Bezalel
text: Leader of the [[Religious Zionist Party]] and Israel's finance minister since December 2022, also serving as a minister in the Defense Ministry with authority over civilian affairs in [[Judea and Samaria]]. A resident of the settlement of Kedumim, he champions settlement growth and opposes a Palestinian state. In 2026 his party ran jointly with Moshe Feiglin's Zehut and won six seats.

name: Ben-Gvir, Itamar
text: Leader of [[Otzma Yehudit]] and national security minister, in charge of the police, since December 2022. A lawyer from Kiryat Arba near [[Hebron]], he was active in his youth in Rabbi Meir Kahane's Kach movement. He quit the government in January 2025 in protest at the Gaza ceasefire and returned that March. His party ran on its own in 2026 and won seven seats.

name: Deri, Aryeh
text: Leader of [[Shas]], the Sephardi ultra-Orthodox party, from 1990 to 1999 and again since 2013. He became interior minister in 1988, was convicted of bribery in 1999 and served time in prison. After a 2022 plea deal on tax offences, the Supreme Court ruled in January 2023 that he could not serve as a minister. Shas fell from 11 seats to six in the 2026 election.

name: Asher, Yaakov
text: Haredi politician who was mayor of Bnei Brak from 2008 to 2013 and has sat in the Knesset for [[United Torah Judaism]] in 2013–2015 and since 2016. In September 2026 Rabbi [[Dov Lando]] chose him to replace Moshe Gafni at the head of Degel HaTorah's slate, which also made him chairman of United Torah Judaism. Under his leadership the party won seven seats and declined to recommend [[Benjamin Netanyahu]] for prime minister.

name: Abbas, Mansour
text: Leader of [[Ra'am]], the United Arab List, since 2019. In 2021 he made Ra'am the first Arab party to join an Israeli governing coalition, in the government of [[Naftali Bennett]] and [[Yair Lapid]]. Ra'am won eight seats in the 2026 election, and Abbas recommended [[Gadi Eisenkot]] for prime minister.

name: Tibi, Ahmad
text: Arab Israeli politician and physician from Taibe who founded the Ta'al party and has sat in the Knesset since 1999, for many years as a deputy speaker. In the 1990s he was an adviser to [[Yasser Arafat]]. He is a leader of the [[Joint List]], which won 11 seats in 2026 and backed [[Gadi Eisenkot]]'s bid to replace the Knesset speaker.

name: Jabareen, Yousef
text: Arab Israeli legal scholar from Umm al-Fahm and a former Knesset member who heads the Hadash party and the [[Joint List]]. He was elected Hadash chairman in May 2026, after Ayman Odeh stepped aside, and led the Joint List to 11 seats in the October 2026 election.

name: Gantz, Benny
text: IDF Chief of Staff from 2011 to 2015 who led the Blue and White alliance, which ran neck and neck with [[Likud]] in three elections in 2019 and 2020. He was defense minister and alternate prime minister from 2020 to 2022 and joined the war cabinet after the [[October 7 attack (2023)]], leaving it in June 2024. With his party polling below the threshold, he withdrew from the 2026 election eight days before the vote.

name: Sa'ar, Gideon
text: Lawyer and Likud veteran who was education minister and interior minister, left the party in 2020 to found New Hope, and served as justice minister in the 2021–2022 government. He rejoined [[Benjamin Netanyahu]]'s coalition in 2024 and has been foreign minister since November 2024. New Hope merged back into [[Likud]] in 2025, and Sa'ar ran on the Likud list in 2026.

name: Katz, Israel
text: Likud veteran who has served as minister of agriculture, transport, intelligence, finance, energy and foreign affairs. He became defense minister in November 2024, replacing Yoav Gallant, and held the post through the later stages of the wars with Hamas, Hezbollah and Iran.

name: Cohen, Eli (politician)
text: Likud minister who was foreign minister in 2023–2024 and later energy minister, after earlier terms as economy minister and intelligence minister. He topped the Likud primary in August 2026, taking the first place on the list after [[Benjamin Netanyahu]].

name: Levin, Yariv
text: Likud lawyer and politician who was speaker of the Knesset in 2020–2021 and has been justice minister and deputy prime minister since December 2022. He is the architect of the government's 2023 judicial overhaul, which set off months of mass protests, and he campaigned in 2026 to complete it.

name: Ohana, Amir
text: Likud politician who became Israel's first openly gay cabinet minister as justice minister in 2019 and later served as public security minister. He has been speaker of the Knesset since December 2022. After the 2026 election, 67 Knesset members asked for a vote to replace him with Matan Kahana of [[Yashar!]], set for November 17, 2026.

name: Yashar!
text: Liberal Zionist party founded on September 16, 2025 by former Chief of Staff [[Gadi Eisenkot]] after he left National Unity. In its first election, in October 2026, it won 21 seats, second only to [[Likud]], and it leads the four-party bloc seeking to replace [[Benjamin Netanyahu]].

name: Together (B'Yachad)
text: Joint list formed on April 26, 2026 by former prime ministers [[Naftali Bennett]] and [[Yair Lapid]], merging Bennett's new party with [[Yesh Atid]] under Bennett's leadership, with Yesh Atid receiving 40 percent of the places. It polled close to Likud at first but won 12 seats in the October 2026 election.

name: Yesh Atid
text: Centrist party founded by [[Yair Lapid]] in 2012; the name means "There Is a Future". It won 19 seats in its first election in 2013, ran within the Blue and White alliance in 2019–2020, and was the largest party in the 2021–2022 coalition. After winning 24 seats in 2022 it led the opposition, and in 2026 it ran as part of [[Together (B'Yachad)]].

name: Joint List
text: Alliance of Arab-majority parties, first formed in 2015, that won a record 15 seats in 2020 before breaking apart. Hadash, Ta'al and Balad revived it for 2026 without [[Ra'am]], led by Hadash chairman [[Yousef Jabareen]] with [[Ahmad Tibi]]. The Central Elections Committee barred it in September 2026, but the Supreme Court reinstated it the same day. It won 11 seats, and with Ra'am gave Arab-led parties a record 19.

name: Ra'am
text: The United Arab List, the political arm of the southern branch of Israel's Islamic Movement, led by [[Mansour Abbas]]. In 2021 it became the first Arab party to join an Israeli governing coalition. Running separately from the [[Joint List]] in 2026, it won eight seats.

name: Democrats (Israel)
text: Center-left party formed in 2024 when the Labor Party, heir to the movement that led Israel's founding generation, merged with Meretz under [[Yair Golan]]. It won eight seats in the 2026 election and belongs to the bloc backing [[Gadi Eisenkot]].

name: Yisrael Beiteinu
text: Secular right-wing party founded in 1999 by [[Avigdor Liberman]], with deep roots among immigrants from the former Soviet Union. It campaigns for drafting ultra-Orthodox men and for civil marriage. It won seven seats in the 2026 election.

name: Otzma Yehudit
text: Far-right party led by [[Itamar Ben-Gvir]]; the name means "Jewish Power". Founded in 2012 by followers of the banned Kach movement, it entered government after the 2022 election, in which it ran jointly with the [[Religious Zionist Party]], and Ben-Gvir became national security minister. It ran alone in 2026 and won seven seats.

name: United Torah Judaism
text: Alliance since 1992 of the two Ashkenazi ultra-Orthodox parties, the Hasidic Agudat Yisrael and the Lithuanian Degel HaTorah, each guided by a council of rabbis. In 2025 it left [[Benjamin Netanyahu]]'s government after a law exempting yeshiva students from military service failed to pass. Led in 2026 by [[Yaakov Asher]], it won seven seats and declined to recommend Netanyahu for prime minister.

name: Shas
text: Sephardi and Mizrahi ultra-Orthodox party founded in 1984 under the spiritual guidance of Rabbi Ovadia Yosef and led for most of its history by [[Aryeh Deri]]. A partner in most governments since the late 1980s, it focuses on religious services, welfare and exemptions from military service for yeshiva students. It fell from 11 seats to six in the 2026 election.

name: Religious Zionist Party
text: Party of the national-religious and settler camp led by [[Bezalel Smotrich]]. Running with [[Otzma Yehudit]] and Noam in 2022, it won 14 seats and joined [[Benjamin Netanyahu]]'s government, with Smotrich as finance minister. In 2026 it ran with Moshe Feiglin's Zehut and won six seats.

name: Kushner, Jared
text: American businessman and son-in-law of President Donald Trump. As senior adviser in Trump's first term he led the talks that produced the [[Abraham Accords]] in 2020. In Trump's second term he helped negotiate the October 2025 Gaza ceasefire, sits on the Board of Peace for Gaza, and was named special envoy for peace in February 2026. The Jerusalem Post ranked him and Ivanka Trump first among the most influential Jews of 2026.

name: Witkoff, Steve
text: New York real-estate developer and longtime friend of Donald Trump who became the US special envoy to the Middle East in 2025. He was a key architect of the Gaza ceasefire that took effect on October 10, 2025, has led US talks with Russia and Iran, and sits on the Board of Peace for Gaza.

name: Lauder, Ronald
text: American businessman and philanthropist, heir to the Estée Lauder company and a former US ambassador to Austria. He has been president of the World Jewish Congress since 2007, and his foundation supports Jewish schools and community life across Central and Eastern Europe. In 2026 he said he will not seek another term when his mandate ends in 2029.

name: Adelson, Miriam
text: Israeli-born physician and philanthropist, widow of the casino owner Sheldon Adelson, whose family controls Las Vegas Sands. She owns the Israeli daily Israel Hayom and has given heavily to [[Yad Vashem]], [[Taglit-Birthright Israel]] and the medical school at Ariel University. She received the US Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2018.

name: Zelensky, Volodymyr
text: President of Ukraine since 2019 and the country's first Jewish president, a former comedian and actor. He has led Ukraine's resistance since Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022. Members of his family were murdered in the [[Holocaust]], and his grandfather fought in the Red Army in the Second World War.

name: Sheinbaum, Claudia
text: President of Mexico since October 2024, the first woman and the first person of Jewish heritage to hold the office. A physicist and environmental engineer, she was mayor of Mexico City from 2018 to 2023. Her grandparents were Jewish immigrants from Lithuania and Bulgaria.

name: Schumer, Chuck
text: US senator from New York since 1999 and Senate Democratic leader since 2017, the highest-ranking Jewish elected official in American history. He was majority leader from 2021 to 2025. After Democrats won the Senate in the November 2026 midterm elections he sought another term as leader, despite opposition from some colleagues and newly elected senators.

name: Shapiro, Josh
text: Governor of Pennsylvania since 2023, an observant Jew and former state attorney general. In April 2025 an arsonist set fire to the governor's residence hours after his family's Passover seder. He won a second term on November 3, 2026 and is widely mentioned as a presidential candidate for 2028.

name: Ackman, Bill
text: American hedge-fund manager who founded Pershing Square Capital Management. After the [[October 7 attack (2023)]] he became one of the most prominent business voices against antisemitism on US college campuses, pressing for the resignation of Harvard's president in early 2024.

name: Greenblatt, Jonathan
text: CEO and national director of the Anti-Defamation League since 2015, succeeding Abraham Foxman. A former White House aide and social entrepreneur, he leads the ADL's tracking of antisemitic incidents and its campaigns against hate online and on campus.

name: Deutch, Ted
text: CEO of the American Jewish Committee since October 2022. Before that he represented south Florida in the US House of Representatives for twelve years, where he chaired the subcommittee on the Middle East.

name: Sharansky, Natan
text: Soviet Jewish refusenik and human-rights activist who spent nine years in Soviet prisons before his release and immigration to Israel in 1986, a symbol of the movement that led to the [[Aliyah from the Soviet Union]]. In Israel he founded the Yisrael BaAliyah party, served as a minister in several governments, and chaired the [[Jewish Agency for Israel]] from 2009 to 2018.

name: Mirvis, Ephraim
text: Chief Rabbi of the United Hebrew Congregations of the Commonwealth since 2013, the leading Orthodox rabbinic voice in Britain. Born in South Africa, he was earlier chief rabbi of Ireland and led congregations in London before succeeding Lord Jonathan Sacks.

name: Jacobs, Rick
text: President of the Union for Reform Judaism since 2012, leading the largest Jewish movement in North America, with about 850 congregations. A former pulpit rabbi in Scarsdale, New York, he is known for work on social justice and disaster relief.

name: Lando, Dov
text: Head of the Slabodka yeshiva in Bnei Brak and, with Rabbi Moshe Hillel Hirsch, spiritual leader of the Lithuanian ultra-Orthodox community and its Degel HaTorah party. In May 2026 he declared that the party no longer trusted [[Benjamin Netanyahu]] and told its lawmakers to dissolve the Knesset, and in September 2026 he replaced its veteran leaders with [[Yaakov Asher]].

name: Krinsky, Yehuda
text: Chairman of Merkos L'Inyonei Chinuch and Machne Israel, the educational and social-service arms of the Chabad-Lubavitch movement, and for decades a secretary to the Lubavitcher Rebbe, Rabbi Menachem Mendel Schneerson. He oversees a worldwide network of thousands of Chabad emissaries and their centers.

name: Dayan, Dani
text: Chairman of [[Yad Vashem]] since 2021. Born in Buenos Aires, he was earlier a technology entrepreneur, chairman of the Yesha Council of settlements and Israel's consul general in New York. From 2025 to early 2026 he also chaired the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance.

name: Dershowitz, Alan
text: American lawyer and Harvard Law School professor emeritus, among the best-known defenders of Israel in American public life. He has written many books, including The Case for Israel (2003), and has represented clients ranging from O. J. Simpson to Donald Trump.

name: Lipstadt, Deborah
text: American historian of the [[Holocaust]] at Emory University who defeated the Holocaust denier David Irving's libel suit against her in a London court in 2000. She served as the US special envoy to monitor and combat antisemitism from 2022 to 2025.

name: Soloveichik, Meir
text: Orthodox rabbi of Congregation Shearith Israel in New York, the oldest Jewish congregation in the United States, and director of the Straus Center for Torah and Western Thought at Yeshiva University. A member of the Soloveitchik rabbinic family, he writes widely on Judaism, Zionism and American political thought.
